hints: Think about what the word dynamic tells you, that both the forward and reverse reactions are still happening and have not stopped.
Think about what you would actually observe if concentrations are no longer changing, even though particles are still reacting.
walkthrough:
Picture what dynamic really means**
Imagine two escalators moving in opposite directions at exactly the same speed. People are constantly moving, but the total number of people on each floor never changes. In a reversible reaction, both $\text{Fe}^{3+} + \text{SCN}^{-} \rightleftharpoons \text{FeSCN}^{2+}$ directions keep happening, they do not stop.

Link equal rates to constant concentrations**
Because the forward reaction makes $\text{FeSCN}^{2+}$ exactly as fast as the reverse reaction breaks it down, there is no overall change. So $[\text{Fe}^{3+}]$, $[\text{SCN}^{-}]$ and $[\text{FeSCN}^{2+}]$ stay constant, and any measurable property such as colour or pressure stays constant too.

Final answer: Rates of forward and reverse reactions are equal.
Concentrations of reactants and products remain constant (no change in measurable properties).

hints: Identify which ion concentration is suddenly increased when solid $\text{KSCN}$ dissolves and how the system can use up that extra ion.
Use the colours given, yellow $\text{Fe}^{3+}$, colourless $\text{SCN}^{-}$ and red $\text{FeSCN}^{2+}$, to decide which colour will become stronger if more red product forms.
Recall which single factor can change the value of $K_{c}$ and whether adding more reactant counts as that factor.
walkthrough:
Spot the disturbance**
Dissolving $\text{KSCN(s)}$ adds extra $\text{SCN}^{-}\text{(aq)}$, which is colourless. You have suddenly increased $[\text{SCN}^{-}]$ on the left of $\text{Fe}^{3+}\text{(aq)} + \text{SCN}^{-}\text{(aq)} \rightleftharpoons \text{FeSCN}^{2+}\text{(aq)}$.

Predict the shift to oppose the change**
To use up the added $\text{SCN}^{-}$, the equilibrium shifts to the right, making more red $\text{FeSCN}^{2+}$. That is why the mixture looks darker red. At the same time $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ is used up in forming that extra product, so $[\text{Fe}^{3+}]$ falls compared with the original mixture.

Remember what controls $K_{c}$**
$K_{c}$ changes only with temperature. Here temperature is stated to be the same, and you only changed concentration. The ratio $$K_{c} = \frac{[\text{FeSCN}^{2+}]}{[\text{Fe}^{3+}][\text{SCN}^{-}]}$$ must return to the same value once the new equilibrium is reached, so $K_{c}$ is unchanged.

Final answer: change in appearance: becomes darker red / more red.
change in relative concentration of $\text{Fe}^{3+}(\text{aq})$: decreases.
change in value of $K_{c}$: no change / remains constant.

hints: Start by converting the initial moles of $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ and $\text{SCN}^{-}$ into initial concentrations using the total volume of $25.0 \text{ cm}^{3}$.
Set up how much of each reactant is used up to make the known equilibrium concentration of $\text{FeSCN}^{2+}$, using the 1:1:1 mole ratio.
Substitute the three equilibrium concentrations into the given $K_{c}$ expression to find the numerical value.
Work out the units for $K_{c}$ by cancelling concentration units in the expression, top divided by bottom squared.
walkthrough:
Find the starting concentrations**
You mix $5.00 \times 10^{-5} \text{ mol}$ of each reactant in $25.0 \text{ cm}^{3} = 0.0250 \text{ dm}^{3}$. So $$[\text{Fe}^{3+}]_{initial} = \frac{5.00 \times 10^{-5}}{0.0250} = 2.00 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$$ and $[\text{SCN}^{-}]_{initial}$ is exactly the same.

Subtract what reacted**
The equation is 1:1:1, so making $4.23 \times 10^{-4} \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ of $\text{FeSCN}^{2+}$ must use up $4.23 \times 10^{-4} \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ of each reactant. At equilibrium: $$[\text{Fe}^{3+}]_{eq} = 0.00200 - 0.000423 = 0.001577 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$$ and $[\text{SCN}^{-}]_{eq}$ is identical.

Plug into the $K_{c}$ expression**
Now substitute: $$K_{c} = \frac{4.23 \times 10^{-4}}{(0.001577)^{2}} = 170$$ to three significant figures. This large value over 1 fits with a good yield of red product.

Sort out the units**
Top has $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$, bottom has $(\text{mol dm}^{-3})^{2}$. Cancelling one set leaves $$\text{units} = \frac{1}{\text{mol dm}^{-3}} = \text{mol}^{-1} \text{dm}^{3}$$ So $K_{c} = 170 \text{ mol}^{-1} \text{dm}^{3}$.

Final answer: Initial $[\text{Fe}^{3+}]$ = initial $[\text{SCN}^{-}]$ = $2.00 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$.
Equilibrium $[\text{Fe}^{3+}]$ = equilibrium $[\text{SCN}^{-}]$ = $1.58 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$.
$K_{c}$ = $170$ with units $\text{mol}^{-1} \text{dm}^{3}$.

hints: Start from the full configuration of an Fe atom and remember that the 4s electrons are removed before the 3d electrons when forming positive ions.
walkthrough:
Remove electrons in the correct order**
Fe is atomic number 26, so Fe atom is $1\text{s}^{2} 2\text{s}^{2} 2\text{p}^{6} 3\text{s}^{2} 3\text{p}^{6} 3\text{d}^{6} 4\text{s}^{2}$. To make $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ you remove three electrons, first both $4\text{s}$ electrons and then one $3\text{d}$ electron. That leaves $$1\text{s}^{2} 2\text{s}^{2} 2\text{p}^{6} 3\text{s}^{2} 3\text{p}^{6} 3\text{d}^{5}$$ which is a stable half filled d subshell.

hints: Count the total outer electrons available, including the extra electron for the 1- charge, and think about how S-C-N can share to give octets with a triple bond on one side.
After placing the bonding pairs, distribute the remaining electrons as lone pairs so that S ends up with three lone pairs, N with one lone pair, and C with none.
walkthrough:
Place the bonding electrons**
In $\text{SCN}^{-}$, carbon is central. Put 2 electrons (one shared pair, a single bond) in the S and C overlap, and 6 electrons (three shared pairs, a triple bond) in the C and N overlap. That uses the bonding framework $\text{S-C}\equiv\text{N}$ and gives every atom a share in an octet.

Add the lone pairs to complete octets**
Now fill the non bonding electrons. Sulfur needs 6 more electrons to complete its octet, so draw 3 lone pairs around S. Nitrogen already shares 6 electrons, so it needs just 2 more electrons, draw 1 lone pair on N. Carbon has 8 electrons around it from the 4 shared pairs, so it has no lone pairs. The whole diagram sits inside square brackets with a minus charge.

Final answer: C to N: 6 shared electrons (triple bond) shown in overlap; C to S: 2 shared electrons (single bond) shown in overlap.
3 lone pairs on S, 0 lone pairs on C, 1 lone pair on N.
